newsitem.title: CANADA: Manitoba evacuates 17,500 people as flood rises.
newsitem.headline: Manitoba evacuates 17,500 people as flood rises.

text.p: Manitoba on Wednesday ordered 17,500 people to evacuate their homes along the swelling Red River as a second boy was presumed drowned in the rising flood waters.

Adam Young, 14, of Winnipeg, was presumed dead after being swept away by powerful currents in a drainage ditch in Winnipeg on Tuesday, police said. Rescue workers resumed the search for Young's body on Wednesday.
On Sunday a four-year-old boy drowned while playing in a culvert along the Assiniboine River which drains into the Red.

About 17,000 residents of the Red River Valley between the U.S. border and Winnipeg were ordered out of their homes early on Wednesday, Manitoba Emergency Management Organization spokesman Ed Peters said.

"Because of the high temperatures of the last few days, the watershed and tributaries are flooding faster. The evacuations are taking place because the rising waters are expected to cut off access to these communities," Peters said.
Meanwhile, 500 Winnipeggers with homes on low ground were ordered out of their homes on Tuesday, Winnipeg Streets and Transportation spokesman Bob McDonald said.
"I was told last night I might have to evacuate. Better safe than sorry, I guess. If I can get extra sandbags I will. I don't know if I can get any," south Winnipeg resident Rob Diziak said.
Canada's Defense Minister Doug Young, who surveyed the flood zone late on Tuesday, said the flooding was worse than he had imagined.
Pledging federal financial support for Manitoba, Young said: "We will provide the government of Manitoba with the complete flexibility in choosing the compensation formula that is most appropriate."
The Canadian government put 10 military helicopters and 17 zodiac boats at Manitoba's disposal.
Manitoba declared a state of emergency on Tuesday, giving provincial officials sweeping powers to seize property, order people to work on emergency projects, ban travel and forcibly evacuate people.

Some 1.5 million sandbags were flown to Winnipeg on Tuesday by Canadian Armed Forces aircraft from Edmonton, Alberta. The flood-stricken city of Fargo, N.D. was trucking 75,000 bags to Winnipeg, about 60 miles (96.56 km) north of the U.S. border.
Winnipeg, the provincial capital, has more than 630,000 residents.

Floods in 1950 and 1979 left 400 square miles (1,036 sq km) of land between the U.S. border and Winnipeg under water. This year's flood may cover double that area and take weeks to drain, emergency officials said.
